title: The LORD Is Slow to Anger and Great in Power
summary: Nahum's oracle against Nineveh opens with a hymn to the LORD as a jealous and avenging God who rules storm, sea, and mountain, yet who is slow to anger, good, and a stronghold for those who trust him. God announces that Nineveh's plots will come to an end, that its gods and its name will be cut off, and that Judah's yoke will be broken. The chapter ends with a messenger on the mountains bringing news of peace.
story: The Minor Prophets have already shown Assyria as the great threat of the eighth century: the rod of God's anger against Samaria, and the invader Micah saw at Judah's gates. Jonah told of a moment when Nineveh repented and God relented. Nahum comes later, when Assyria's cruelty has continued for generations, and announces its end. This opening chapter lays the theological foundation for what follows. Before any chariot appears, the reader learns who God is: powerful over all creation, patient but not indifferent, fierce toward his enemies, and tender toward those who take refuge in him. The rest of the book, with its battle scenes and taunts, is meant to be read in the light of this chapter.
historical:
Nahum spoke sometime between the fall of Thebes in Egypt (about 663 BC), which he mentions in 3:8-10, and the fall of Nineveh in 612 BC. For most of that period Assyria dominated the Near East, and Judah, under Manasseh and then Amon, was its vassal, paying tribute and living under its shadow. A generation earlier, in 701 BC, Sennacherib had devastated Judah's towns and besieged Jerusalem, and verse 11's plotter of evil against the LORD may recall that king, whose envoys had mocked the God of Israel (2 Kings 18 to 19), or it may describe Assyrian kingship in general.

The promise that Judah's yoke will be broken fits the years when Assyrian power began to crack. After Ashurbanipal's death, Babylon under Nabopolassar rose against Assyria, and the Medes joined the attack. In 612 BC Nineveh fell. Verse 8 speaks of an overwhelming flood making an end of the city; the image is traditional language for irresistible judgment, but Nineveh did sit on the Tigris with the Khosr River running through it, and some scholars connect the image with the role water may have played in the city's fall, a question taken up in chapter 2.
cultural:
The opening hymn draws on imagery shared across the ancient Near East, where storm gods were pictured riding the clouds and rebuking the sea. Israel's poets used the same pictures to say that the LORD alone commands the forces others worshiped (compare Psalm 18 and Psalm 29). Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon were the most fertile and forested regions of the land, famous for pasture, orchards, and cedars; if even they wither, nothing can stand. The book's first word, burden or oracle (massa), was a common heading for prophetic words against nations, and the book also calls itself a written scroll, one of the few prophetic books to do so at its start.

Verse 14 strikes at the heart of Assyrian pride. Kings in the ancient world set great store by their name and descendants, and Assyrian kings filled their palaces and temples with inscriptions and statues to preserve their memory. God declares that Nineveh's name will not be carried on and that its carved images will be removed from the house of its gods. Verse 15 then shifts to a scene every ancient reader knew: a runner coming over the hills with news from the battlefield. Here the news is peace, and Judah is told to celebrate its feasts and keep its vows, the ordinary rhythms of worship that foreign domination had disturbed.
literary: Verses 2 to 8 form a hymn that many scholars recognize as a partial alphabetic acrostic, with successive lines beginning with letters in the order of the Hebrew alphabet from the first letter through roughly the eleventh, though the pattern is irregular and may have been loosened in transmission. The hymn is framed by God's character: jealous and avenging at the start, good and a stronghold in the middle, with the famous line from Exodus 34:7 set within it. Verses 9 to 15 then alternate between address to Nineveh and address to Judah, and the shifts can be abrupt because the speaker turns from one audience to the other without warning. Translations supply names (O Nineveh, O Judah) to help the reader follow. Verse 15 in English is 2:1 in the Hebrew Bible, where it opens the next section; English Bibles attach it to chapter 1 as its climax.

outline.t: The jealous, avenging God who shakes creation
A stronghold for those who trust, an end for his enemies
Nineveh's plotting will come to nothing
Nineveh's name and gods cut off
Good news of peace on the mountains

doctrines.note: God's jealousy is his rightful zeal for his people and his own honor, not petty envy. The chapter holds together his patience (slow to anger), his power, his justice (he will not leave the guilty unpunished), and his goodness to those who trust him, all drawn from his self-revelation to Moses.

God's vengeance here is judicial: the response of the world's rightful king to an empire that plotted against him and crushed other peoples. It is directed at his enemies, not at the helpless, and its purpose includes the rescue of the oppressed.
Sea, rivers, mountains, and empires all respond to God. Assyria's alliances and numbers cannot protect it, because the LORD has issued a command concerning it.

words.note: Qanno, jealous. This form appears only here and in Joshua 24:19, though related words are common. Applied to God, jealousy is the passion of a husband or a king for an exclusive, rightful relationship. It explains why God acts against Nineveh: its violence has struck at the people he has bound to himself.

Naqam, to avenge, used three times in verse 2. In the Old Testament, vengeance belongs properly to God, who acts as judge to restore justice; the law forbade personal revenge (Leviticus 19:18). The repetition stresses that the wrongs done by Assyria will be answered, but by God, not by Judah's own hand.

Arek, long or slow, in the phrase slow to anger (literally long of nostrils, since anger was pictured as heat in the nose). The phrase comes from Exodus 34:6 and appears in Jonah 4:2, where Jonah complains that God is exactly this toward Nineveh. Nahum affirms God's patience even as he announces that it has limits.

Ma'oz, stronghold or place of safety. Verse 7 sets it in the middle of the hymn of wrath: the same power that shatters rocks is a fortress for those who trust in him. The word is common in the Psalms for God as refuge.

christ: Verse 15 is the chapter's clearest bridge to the New Testament. Its picture of the feet of one who brings good news and proclaims peace closely matches Isaiah 52:7, and Paul quotes Isaiah's version in Romans 10:15, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!”, to describe the preaching of the gospel. In Nahum the good news is the end of an oppressive empire; in the New Testament the same pattern describes the announcement that Christ has defeated sin and death, the powers behind every human tyranny. The hymn's portrait of God also finds its fullest expression in Christ. The one who rebukes the sea in verse 4 is echoed when Jesus rebukes the wind and the waves (Mark 4:39), and the disciples ask who this is. These are thematic connections: Nahum does not predict the Messiah. But the God who is both slow to anger and unwilling to leave the guilty unpunished is the God whose justice and mercy meet at the cross.

hard.q: How can a good God be described as avenging and full of wrath?
hard.a: Many readers are uncomfortable with a God who takes vengeance. There are several ways to understand the language. First, in the Bible vengeance is a legal idea: the act of a just ruler who defends the wronged and punishes the wrongdoer, not the spite of a wounded ego. Second, the chapter balances wrath with patience and goodness: God is slow to anger (verse 3) and a stronghold for those who trust him (verse 7). Third, the object of God's wrath is an empire known from its own records for mass deportation, torture, and plunder; a God indifferent to that would not be good. Some readers still find the intensity of the language troubling and note that the Bible itself contains a wider picture, including God's mercy to Nineveh in Jonah. Others argue that the victims of Assyria would have heard Nahum's words as the long-awaited assurance that their suffering mattered to God. Both responses take the text seriously; neither requires pretending that divine wrath is simple to understand.

questions: The chapter calls God both avenging and slow to anger. How do you tend to picture God, and which of these traits do you find easier to believe?
Verse 7 places God's care for those who trust him in the middle of a hymn about his power. Why might it matter that God's gentleness and his strength belong to the same person?
For Judah, the end of Assyria meant freedom to celebrate its feasts again. What would it mean to you to hear that an oppressive power in your life had been broken?
